name: Diego Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a delivery truck for a drinks wholesaler, so beer kegs, crates and wine cases to pubs, restaurants and hotels around the city. I start at six, load the truck by drop order, and do about fifteen drops, lowering kegs down through the trapdoor into the cellar on a rope and a cushion. I like the pub landlords, they're characters, and you get offered a lot of coffee. The worst part is city-centre parking and the cellars with steep steps, because one slip with a full keg and you've done your back for good.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up doing this?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My uncle was a drayman, which is the old word for it, and he got me the start. I've been driving a year and a half, and I'm still slow, the older lads do the round an hour quicker. I live with my girlfriend Ana, who's a hairdresser, and we've saved about ten months, mostly because neither of us goes out much except church and family on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's how it usually goes, lots of noise and then everybody goes back to work. I'd say it to the landlords over coffee. I'm not one for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job stays, and I can keep learning the trade properly. The pubs would still need someone to bring the kegs down. My worries would be my back and the pubs that keep closing, because fewer pubs means fewer drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the round and ask about the mechanic apprenticeship at our workshop, which I've been thinking about anyway. I'd keep saving with Ana for a wedding and a place. I might use the AI on my phone now and then to check an invoice, like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned pubs closing. How much does that weigh on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three pubs on my round closed this year, and one of them had been there two hundred years. That's people not going out, not robots. If it keeps up, the wholesaler cuts a round, and the newest driver goes first, which is me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the mechanic apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my back won't last forever lifting kegs, and the workshop lads are never short of work. The company runs apprenticeships, which I think is the right way, you learn by doing next to someone who knows. My uncle always said a man with a trade never goes hungry.

say: I'd say there's **lots of noise** and then everyone goes back to **work**.
I'd say it to **pub landlords** over coffee, not online.
think: My **job stays** and I can keep learning the trade properly.
My real worries are my **back** and **pubs closing** on my round.
do: Ask about the **mechanic apprenticeship** at the wholesaler's workshop.
Keep **saving** with my girlfriend for a wedding and a place.
Use **AI** on my phone now and then to check invoices.

fieldNote: His real pressure is **pub closures**, which could cut the newest driver first.
He values **apprenticeships** and learning beside experienced workers.
His **back** is a quiet long-term worry that shapes his plans.

steps.text: Keep doing the fifteen-drop pub and restaurant round
Ask the workshop manager about the mechanic apprenticeship
Save with his girlfriend for a wedding and a flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses should be free to use whatever works, that's how things get better. But I'd also say companies owe it to their people to train them, not just drop them. I'd say it at work and at church, the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the order taking goes first. Our sales rep, the one who visits pubs and takes orders, could be replaced by an app the landlords use. The drops would stay with us, but I'd wonder if the round gets planned so tight there's no time for a coffee and a chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the mechanic apprenticeship this year, because it's the safer trade and the company pays for it. I'd learn the new ordering app once the other drivers had it working. I'd keep saving, maybe a bit more each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not worried for me so much as for how things are going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the wholesaler?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sales rep, a woman called Carmen who's been with the company fifteen years. Landlords love her, she remembers their kids' names. But if the app does the orders, the bosses might say they don't need her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would taking an apprenticeship mean a pay cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, for two years, maybe a few hundred a month less. That's what the savings are for. My girlfriend says she'd rather I take an apprentice's pay cut now than hurt my back at thirty-five.

think: The **order taking** goes first, with landlords using an **app**.

do: Start the **mechanic apprenticeship** this year, paid for by the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast for families to keep up. I don't want handouts, but I'd want companies to keep training people instead of throwing them away. At church I think a lot of people would be scared, and I'd try to be steady for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it shakes me. The ordering and planning go in 2028, and around 2031 the robots could drive and maybe even lift kegs. A city-centre cellar with steep steps is hard for a robot, but I wouldn't bet my wedding on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get into the mechanic apprenticeship straight away and finish it before 2031. I'd keep the savings safe and stop thinking about buying for a while. I'd ask my uncle and the older men at church who've changed trades before for advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be praying more, that's for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is mostly hands-on, so the robots come about three years after the thinking work. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I've got just about long enough to finish an apprenticeship if I start now. If I wait a year to see, I'm too late. So for once I wouldn't wait for the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ana decide about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still get married, that's not about money. But we'd do it small, in the church hall, not a big hotel. The house can wait, a marriage shouldn't.

fieldNote: The tight timeline pushes this **steady** man to act before others for once.
He'd keep the **wedding** but shrink it, putting marriage ahead of property.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning, and sensible people will use it. I'd tell the younger lads at work to get an apprenticeship while they can. I wouldn't blame anyone, it's just how things move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the drops go around 2034, when I'd be thirty-four with a trade by then. The thinking side changes in 2031, which hits the office and the reps more than me. So I'd be alright if I get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch how things go for a year, and then start the apprenticeship in year two. We'd get married next year and buy a small flat. I'd keep saving steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's me, I like to see it working first. If the robot trucks are on the road by 2030, I want to know what the mechanics actually fix on them. No point training on old diesel engines if the new robot trucks are all electric and computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most during those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the older drivers, men in their fifties with no trade. They'd be too young to retire and too set in their ways to start again. I'd want the company to look after them first.

fieldNote: He'd wait to learn **which engines** mechanics will actually fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so nobody should panic or ask for handouts. Work hard, learn a trade, look after your family. That's what I'd say to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm fine in this one. I'd be thirty-nine around 2039, with a trade and probably kids. The office side changing in 2036 doesn't touch me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the round for a few years, get married, and start the apprenticeship when the time feels right, maybe in two or three years. I'd keep saving. Life would go on mostly as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything make you want to move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My back, more than the robots. If it starts going, I'll move to the workshop straight away. The robots are a reason to move to the workshop, but my back is the real clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade, something real you can do with your hands. And stay close to family and church, because that's what holds you up when things change. That's what my parents told me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd only just have time to finish a trade if I started straight away. What would help is companies running proper apprenticeships for their own people, with fair pay while you learn, rather than the government handing out money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the pub landlords. They're small business people too, and a lot of them are hanging on by a thread already. If robots make big pub chains cheaper, the little pubs go, and so do the delivery rounds.

headlineQuote: If robots make big pub chains cheaper, the little pubs go, and so do the delivery rounds.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old** drinks delivery driver who lowers kegs into **pub cellars**.
He and his hairdresser girlfriend have about **ten months** saved and plan to marry.
He is **steady** with tech and waits to see things work, except when time is short.
In every picture his plan is a **mechanic apprenticeship**, partly to save his back.
He moves from **calm** to **anxious** in the fastest picture, trusting trade, family and church.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which leaves barely enough time to finish a **trade**.
whatWouldHelp: Company-run **apprenticeships** with **fair pay** while learning, rather than government money.
